title: Streaming: Structured Streaming and watermarks
goal: By the end you can explain why a stream must be grouped by event time, predict when a windowed count with a watermark writes a window and which late events it drops, pick an output mode for a sink, and say what makes a pipeline from Kafka to an Iceberg table exactly once.

warmup.q: A stream counts authorizations per merchant in 5-minute windows of event time, with `withWatermark("event_time", "10 minutes")`. The latest event seen so far is from 10:14. An authorization stamped 10:03 arrives now. What happens to it?
options: Dropped: it is 11 minutes behind the latest event, more than the 10 minutes allowed
Counted in its window, 10:00 to 10:05, because that window is still open
Counted in the current window, 10:10 to 10:15
The query fails with a late-data error
warmup.why: The watermark is 10:14 minus 10 minutes, 10:04. Spark drops a late event only when its window has closed, meaning the watermark has reached the window's end. [10:00, 10:05) ends at 10:05, after 10:04, so it's still open and the event is counted. The tempting answer judges the event by its own age, which isn't the rule; the stepper in section 3 shows this exact batch.

sections.h: Event time is when the card was used, not when you heard about it
sections.body:
Your fraud team wants a velocity rule: alert when one merchant gets more than 30 card authorizations in 5 minutes. The events come from a Kafka topic. Each event carries the time the card was used, set by the payment service when it authorized the payment. That's the **event time**. The moment your consumer reads the event is the **processing time**. Usually the two are a second apart. Sometimes they aren't.

Version 1 counts what arrives: every 5 minutes, count the events the consumer read in those 5 minutes. It's simple, and it needs no state beyond the current bucket. Now the consumer goes down from 10:10 to 10:20 (a bad deploy, a rebalance storm, a broker failover). Merchant 7 keeps taking one authorization every 20 seconds, and Kafka keeps them. At 10:20 the consumer comes back and reads the 10-minute backlog in about a minute. The Try it runs exactly this. Counted by arrival, the 10:10 and 10:15 buckets are empty and the 10:20 bucket holds 45 events, so the rule fires at a merchant whose real rate never changed. Counted by event time, every 5-minute window holds 15. The outage moved the events in processing time; it didn't change when they happened.

Version 2 groups by event time. Each event goes into the window its own timestamp falls in, whenever it arrives. A tumbling window of 5 minutes is the easiest kind: windows start at 10:00, 10:05, 10:10, and so on, and an event at 10:03:12 belongs to [10:00, 10:05), which includes its start and excludes its end. In Spark it's the same `groupBy` you'd write over a table:

```kotlin
events.groupBy(window(col("event_time"), "5 minutes"), col("merchant_id")).count()
```

Two more shapes use the same function. `window(col("event_time"), "10 minutes", "5 minutes")` makes sliding windows: 10 minutes long, starting every 5, so each event counts in two of them. `session_window(col("event_time"), "5 minutes")` makes one window per burst of activity, closed by 5 quiet minutes.

Event time fixes the counts, and it creates a new problem. In version 1, the 10:00 bucket was finished at 10:05 by definition. In version 2, an event from 10:03 can arrive at 10:20, or tomorrow. When is a window finished? That question drives the rest of this lesson.

try.title: Count a backlog by arrival and by event time
steps: Run `EventTimeDemo`. It builds 30 minutes of authorizations for one merchant, one every 20 seconds, with a consumer outage from 10:10 to 10:20, and counts them per 5 minutes twice: by `arrival_time` and by `event_time`.
Predict the counts in the 10:10, 10:15 and 10:20 windows for both columns before you read them.
Which column would you put a fraud threshold on, and what could still make that column's counts wrong?

code.title: EventTimeDemo.kt
code.src:
package sfz.bigdata.l11.demo

import org.apache.spark.sql.RowFactory
import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.col
import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.date_format
import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.window
import org.apache.spark.sql.types.DataTypes
import org.apache.spark.sql.types.StructType
import java.sql.Timestamp
import java.time.Duration

/**
 * Merchant 7 gets one authorization every 20 seconds from 10:00 to 10:30. The fraud consumer is
 * down from 10:10 to 10:20; when it comes back it reads the backlog in about a minute. Counts per
 * 5 minutes, once by arrival (processing time) and once by when the card was used (event time).
 */
fun main() {
    val spark = demoSpark()
    val outageStart = at("10:10")
    val outageEnd = at("10:20")
    val rows = (0 until 90).map { i ->
        val eventTime = at("10:00").plusSeconds(20L * i)
        val arrival = if (!eventTime.isBefore(outageStart) && eventTime.isBefore(outageEnd)) {
            // the backlog: 10 minutes of events read back in 1 minute, in order
            outageEnd.plusMillis(Duration.between(outageStart, eventTime).toMillis() / 10)
        } else {
            eventTime.plusSeconds(2)                                        // normally a 2-second lag
        }
        RowFactory.create(7, Timestamp.from(eventTime), Timestamp.from(arrival))
    }
    val schema = StructType().add("merchant_id", DataTypes.IntegerType)
        .add("event_time", DataTypes.TimestampType).add("arrival_time", DataTypes.TimestampType)
    val events = spark.createDataFrame(rows, schema)

    fun countBy(column: String) = events.groupBy(window(col(column), "5 minutes")).count()
        .select(date_format(col("window.start"), "HH:mm").alias("w"), col("count"))
        .collectAsList().associate { it.getString(0) to it.getLong(1) }
    val byArrival = countBy("arrival_time")
    val byEvent = countBy("event_time")
    println("window   by arrival time   by event time")
    for (w in (byArrival.keys + byEvent.keys).sorted()) {
        println("%-8s %10d %17d".format(w, byArrival[w] ?: 0, byEvent[w] ?: 0))
    }
    println("events: ${rows.size}; rule \"more than 30 in 5 minutes\" fires on arrival time: " +
        byArrival.filterValues { it > 30 }.keys + ", on event time: " + byEvent.filterValues { it > 30 }.keys)
    spark.stop()
}

```text
window   by arrival time   by event time
10:00            15                15
10:05            15                15
10:10             0                15
10:15             0                15
10:20            45                15
10:25            15                15

```

By arrival time the outage shows up as two empty windows and a spike of 45 at 10:20, and the "more than 30 in 5 minutes" rule fires on it. By event time every window has 15 events, which is what really happened. The event-time count is only as good as the timestamps: a service with a wrong clock, or one that stamps events when it sends them instead of when the card was used, breaks it.

refs.title: Structured Streaming: window operations on event time

sections.h: A streaming query runs your plan again on each new slice of input
sections.body:
Spark's Structured Streaming runs that `groupBy` over a stream with the batch engine you already know from lessons 5 to 7. The model: the input stream is a table that keeps getting new rows, and your query defines a result table over it. Spark doesn't recompute the whole result each time. It runs in **micro-batches**: every trigger (by default, as soon as the previous batch finishes), it asks the source for the new data since last time, the new Kafka offsets for example, runs the plan on just those rows, and combines the result with what it remembered.

For a count per window, "what it remembered" is a running count for every window that might still change. That memory is the **state store**: a key-value store, keyed here by (window, merchant), split into partitions like a shuffle (lesson 6), so each task owns the counts of its keys. In batch 1 of the next section's stepper, three events arrive and the state store gets two entries: window [10:00, 10:05) with count 2 and [10:05, 10:10) with count 1. When batch 2 brings 10:14, Spark reads the matching state, adds one, and writes the new entry. Each batch writes its changes as a new version of the state under the query's checkpoint folder, which section 5 comes back to.

Now the problem from section 1, in numbers. If no window is ever finished, Spark must keep every window's count forever, in case a late event arrives. A payments company with 200,000 active merchants has 288 five-minute windows per merchant per day: up to 57.6 million state entries a day, growing every day. The state store would fill the executors' memory within weeks, and every batch would checkpoint more of it. There's also nothing safe to send downstream: a count that may still change can't be written once to a table or a fraud system.

So a streaming engine needs a rule that says "this window is done": after it, the count is final, it can be written once, and its state can be thrown away. The rule can't wait for certainty, because a late event can always come. It has to be a bet on how late events can be, stated up front. That bet is the watermark.

sections.h: A watermark decides when a window is final
sections.body:
A **watermark** is Spark's running estimate of "event time has reached here, nothing older is still on its way". You set it with one line, on the event-time column, before the aggregation:

```kotlin
events.withWatermark("event_time", "10 minutes")
    .groupBy(window(col("event_time"), "5 minutes"), col("merchant_id"))
    .count()
```

The rule is short. After each micro-batch, Spark takes the latest event time it has seen so far and subtracts the delay you gave: latest 10:14, delay 10 minutes, watermark 10:04. The watermark only moves forward. A window is final once the watermark reaches its end, and then two things happen: the count can be written downstream, and its state is deleted. Step through it below; each frame is a real micro-batch from the Try it.

Three details catch people out, and the stepper shows each one.

First, the new watermark takes effect from the next batch. An event that arrives in the same batch as a big jump in time is judged against the old watermark.

Second, Spark drops a late event because its **window** has closed, not because the event is older than the delay. In batch 3, an event from 10:03 arrives 11 minutes behind the latest event, more than the 10 minutes allowed, and it's still counted, because its window [10:00, 10:05) ends at 10:05 and the watermark is at 10:04. Spark's documentation promises only one direction: data less late than the delay is never dropped, and later data may or may not be aggregated.

Third, the watermark moves only when new events arrive. If the stream goes quiet, the last windows wait, and their counts aren't written until later events push the watermark past their ends.

The delay is your bet, and it trades two costs. A longer delay counts more late events, keeps more windows in state, and writes each final count later. A shorter one writes sooner and drops more. Pick it from data: measure how late your events really are (the difference between processing time and event time), take a high percentile, and watch `numRowsDroppedByWatermark` in the query's progress to see what the bet costs.

package sfz.bigdata.l11.demo

import org.apache.spark.api.java.function.VoidFunction2
import org.apache.spark.sql.Dataset

import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.col

import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.window
import java.io.File
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentLinkedQueue

/**
 * A windowed count with a 10-minute watermark, in append mode. Six batches of events arrive, some
 * out of order and late. After each one, prints the watermark, what append mode wrote, how many
 * windows the state holds and how many events were dropped as too late.
 */
fun main() {
    val spark = demoSpark()
    val events = authorizations(spark)
    val written = ConcurrentLinkedQueue<String>()
    val query = events.toDF()
        .withWatermark("event_time", "10 minutes")
        .groupBy(window(col("event_time"), "5 minutes"))
        .count()
        .select(date_format(col("window.start"), "HH:mm").alias("start"), date_format(col("window.end"), "HH:mm").alias("end"), col("count"))
        .writeStream()
        .outputMode("append")
        .option("checkpointLocation", File(DEMO_DIR, "watermark-checkpoint").absolutePath)
        // print-friendly sink: collect what each micro-batch writes
        .foreachBatch(VoidFunction2<Dataset<Row>, Long> { df, _ ->
            df.collectAsList().forEach { written += "[${it.getString(0)}, ${it.getString(1)}) = ${it.getLong(2)}" }
        })
        .start()

    var batch = 0
    fun step(vararg times: String) {
        val before = query.watermark()
        events.send(*times)
        query.processAllAvailable()
        val ops = query.recentProgress().flatMap { it.stateOperators().toList() }
        val dropped = ops.sumOf { it.numRowsDroppedByWatermark() }
        val inState = query.lastProgress().stateOperators().first().numRowsTotal()
        val out = generateSequence { written.poll() }.toList().sorted()
        println("batch ${++batch}: sent ${times.joinToString(" ")}")
        println("   watermark ${before} -> ${query.watermark()}; append wrote ${if (out.isEmpty()) "nothing" else out.joinToString()}; " +
            "windows in state: $inState; dropped so far: $dropped")
    }
    step("10:01", "10:02", "10:06")
    step("10:14")
    step("10:03")
    step("10:21")
    step("10:04", "10:08")
    step("10:13")
    query.stop()
    spark.stop()
}

refs.title: Structured Streaming: handling late data and watermarking

sections.h: Output modes decide what each batch writes
sections.body:
A windowed count is a result table that keeps changing. The **output mode** says which rows of it each micro-batch hands to the sink.

Append mode writes a row once, when it can no longer change. For a windowed aggregation that means: when the watermark closes the window. It's the only mode that fits sinks that can't change what they've written, such as files and most Iceberg pipelines, and it needs a watermark for any aggregation. The price is latency: the 10:00 window appears only after an event from 10:15 or later has arrived.

Update mode writes every row that changed in this batch, as soon as it changes. The fraud system sees "merchant 7, window 10:00, count 2" right away and "count 3" when the late event arrives. That suits a sink that can upsert by key, such as a key-value store or a `MERGE` in `foreachBatch`. State is still cleaned up by the watermark.

Complete mode writes the whole result table every batch. It's for small results, such as a dashboard's top-10, and it can't drop state, because it has to rewrite every window every time. In the Try it, complete mode even counts the late 10:04 that the other two modes dropped, because it never removes a window from state.

The sink has to agree with the mode. Spark's file sink only appends. Iceberg's streaming sink supports append and complete. Kafka and `foreachBatch` take whatever you give them, and the rest is up to you.

For a fraud velocity alert you want the earliest signal, so use update mode into a store keyed by (merchant, window). For the analytics table of the same counts, use append mode into Iceberg, so each window lands once, final.

refs.title: Structured Streaming: output modes and sinks

sections.h: Exactly once needs a replayable source, a checkpoint and an idempotent sink
sections.body:
A streaming job will crash. What do you get after the restart: every event counted once, some counted twice, some lost? Structured Streaming can give you exactly once from source to sink, but only if three parts each do their share.

The source must be replayable. Kafka is: Spark asks for an offset range, and asking again later returns the same records. Spark doesn't rely on your consumer group's committed offsets for this; it keeps its own.

The checkpoint records progress. Before a batch runs, Spark writes the batch's offset ranges to `offsets/<batch id>` in the checkpoint folder. After the sink has written the batch, Spark writes `commits/<batch id>`. The state store's versions live in `state/`. On restart, Spark finds the last batch with an offsets entry but no commit entry and runs it again, with the same offsets and the same state, so it produces the same output.

That replay is the catch. If the crash came after the sink wrote the batch but before `commits/` recorded it, the sink gets the same output twice. So the sink must be **idempotent**, or transactional. Spark's file sink and Iceberg's sink both are: Iceberg records the query id and the batch id (`spark.sql.streaming.epochId`) in each snapshot's summary, and skips a batch it already committed. In `foreachBatch` you get the batch id and have to use it yourself, for example with a `MERGE` keyed on the window, or by writing the batch id next to the data. A plain `INSERT` is at-least-once. Spark's Kafka sink is at-least-once too. The Try it fakes exactly that crash: the Parquet folder written by a naive `foreachBatch` ends with 4 rows, the Iceberg table with 2.

This is the standard path from Kafka to the lakehouse: a Structured Streaming job reads the topic, aggregates or cleans, and appends to Iceberg every minute or so. Each batch is one commit, so a one-minute trigger makes 1,440 snapshots a day, plus at least one small file per partition for every batch that writes rows. Schedule lesson 10's compaction and expiry from day one.

Two newer options sit next to micro-batches. Spark 4.1 added Real-time Mode for stateless queries, and Spark 4.3 extended it to aggregations and other stateful ones. It runs long-lived tasks that process records as they come, for latencies in milliseconds instead of hundreds of milliseconds. It reads only from Kafka and doesn't write to Iceberg. Apache Flink was built streaming-first. It handles each event as it arrives, keeps very large keyed state (Flink 2.0 can keep it on object storage), and offers exactly-once into Kafka through transactions. Choose Flink when streaming is the product: large state, per-event latency, many long-running pipelines. Stay with Spark when your team already runs it and seconds of latency are fine.

package sfz.bigdata.l11.demo

import org.apache.spark.api.java.function.VoidFunction2
import org.apache.spark.sql.Dataset
import org.apache.spark.sql.Row
import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.col
import org.apache.spark.sql.functions.window
import org.apache.spark.sql.streaming.StreamingQuery
import java.io.File

/**
 * One windowed count, written by two queries with their own checkpoints: one to an Iceberg table,
 * one through foreachBatch to a plain Parquet folder (append, ignoring the batch id). Then a
 * crash is faked between "the sink wrote" and "the commit log says so", and both restart.
 */
fun main() {
    val spark = demoSpark()
    val events = authorizations(spark)
    val counts = events.toDF()
        .withWatermark("event_time", "10 minutes")
        .groupBy(window(col("event_time"), "5 minutes"), col("merchant_id"))
        .count()
        .select(col("window.start").alias("window_start"), col("merchant_id"), col("count").alias("authorizations"))
    spark.sql("CREATE TABLE lake.pay.auth_counts (window_start TIMESTAMP, merchant_id INT, authorizations BIGINT) USING iceberg")
    val icebergCheckpoint = File(DEMO_DIR, "checkpoint-iceberg")
    val folderCheckpoint = File(DEMO_DIR, "checkpoint-folder")
    val folder = File(DEMO_DIR, "auth-counts-parquet")

    fun startIceberg(): StreamingQuery = counts.writeStream().format("iceberg").outputMode("append")
        .option("checkpointLocation", icebergCheckpoint.absolutePath).toTable("lake.pay.auth_counts")
    fun startFolder(): StreamingQuery = counts.writeStream().outputMode("append")
        .option("checkpointLocation", folderCheckpoint.absolutePath)
        // a sink that is NOT idempotent: it appends whatever the batch holds, ignoring the batch id
        .foreachBatch(VoidFunction2<Dataset<Row>, Long> { df, _ -> df.write().mode("append").parquet(folder.absolutePath) })
        .start()
    fun rows(): String {
        val ice = spark.table("lake.pay.auth_counts").count()
        val par = if (folder.exists()) spark.read().parquet(folder.absolutePath).count() else 0
        return "Iceberg table $ice rows, Parquet folder $par rows"
    }
    fun logs(dir: File, name: String) = File(dir, name).list()!!.filter { !it.startsWith(".") }.map { it.toInt() }.sorted()

    var ice = startIceberg()
    var par = startFolder()
    for (b in listOf(listOf("10:01", "10:02", "10:06"), listOf("10:21"))) {
        events.send(*b.toTypedArray())
        ice.processAllAvailable()
        par.processAllAvailable()
    }
    println("before the crash: ${rows()}")
    println("checkpoint: offsets ${logs(icebergCheckpoint, "offsets")}, commits ${logs(icebergCheckpoint, "commits")}, " +
        "state/ holds ${File(icebergCheckpoint, "state").walkTopDown().count { it.isFile && it.name.endsWith(".delta") }} delta files")
    println("offsets/3 starts with: " + File(icebergCheckpoint, "offsets/3").readLines()[1].substringBefore(",\"conf\"") + "}")
    ice.stop()
    par.stop()

    // the crash: both sinks wrote batch 3, but the process died before the commit log recorded it
    for (dir in listOf(icebergCheckpoint, folderCheckpoint)) {
        val last = logs(dir, "commits").last()
        File(dir, "commits/$last").delete()
        File(dir, "commits/.$last.crc").delete()
    }
    println("deleted commits/3 in both checkpoints; restarting")
    ice = startIceberg()
    par = startFolder()
    ice.processAllAvailable()
    par.processAllAvailable()
    println("after the restart, Spark ran batch ${ice.recentProgress().first().batchId()} again: ${rows()}")
    println("Iceberg snapshots by epoch: " + spark.sql(
        "SELECT summary['spark.sql.streaming.epochId'] AS epoch, coalesce(summary['added-records'], '0') AS added " +
            "FROM lake.pay.auth_counts.snapshots ORDER BY committed_at").collectAsList().joinToString { "${it.getString(0)}:+${it.getString(1)}" })
    ice.stop()
    par.stop()

refs.title: Structured Streaming: fault tolerance and exactly-once semantics

analogy: A watermark works like the cut-off for a daily settlement batch. The acquirer says: we close the 2 November file once we've seen transactions stamped 3 November 02:00, because almost nothing for 2 November arrives later than that. Transactions for 2 November that come in before the cut-off go into the file. Ones that come after it go to an exception queue, or are lost if nobody built one. The cut-off isn't based on the wall clock; it moves when later transactions show up, which is why a quiet day closes late. The file, once sent, is never resent: that's append mode. The analogy breaks at the boundary. A settlement cut-off is about the transaction's own date, while Spark judges a late event by its window: an event older than the delay still gets in if its window hasn't closed yet.
in_your_world: You already run Kafka consumers, and the processing-time trap is the bug you've seen when a consumer group rebalances or a deploy stalls it: lag builds, then the consumer drains it in a burst, and anything that counts per minute of arrival spikes. A Structured Streaming job reading the same topic should count by the authorization's own timestamp, set by your Quarkus service when it called the issuer, with a watermark sized from your real consumer lag (your Kafka lag dashboards already show the 99th percentile). The exactly-once rules map onto what you do by hand today: Kafka is the replayable source, the checkpoint plays the role of committed offsets, and an idempotent sink is the same idea as the idempotency key on your payment API. A sink that doesn't use the batch id is at-least-once, like a consumer that commits offsets after it writes.
mistake: The common mistake is putting the watermark on the wrong thing, or not at all. Without `withWatermark`, a windowed count in update or complete mode runs fine in testing and then keeps every window of every merchant in state forever, until the executors run out of memory weeks later. With a watermark on a different column from the window, or added after the aggregation, Spark can't use it to finalize windows, and an append-mode query is rejected at start. People do it because the batch version of the query needs no watermark, so the streaming version looks complete without one. The fix: call `withWatermark` on the same event-time column the window uses, before the `groupBy`; size the delay from measured lateness; and watch two numbers in the query's progress, the state's row count (it should level off) and `numRowsDroppedByWatermark` (it should stay small).

worked.title: From a Kafka topic to an Iceberg table of fraud counts

steps.say: Read the topic. Kafka gives you bytes, so parse the JSON value into columns and keep the authorization's own timestamp as the event time. `startingOffsets` applies only to the very first run; after that the checkpoint decides.
steps.code:
val raw = spark.readStream()
    .format("kafka")
    .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", "kafka:9092")
    .option("subscribe", "card-authorizations")
    .option("startingOffsets", "earliest")
    .load()
val events = raw.select(from_json(col("value").cast("string"), AUTH_SCHEMA).alias("a"))
    .select(col("a.merchant_id"), col("a.authorized_at").alias("event_time"))

steps.say: Count by event time, with a watermark on the same column, before the aggregation. The delay comes from measured lateness: here, the 99.9th percentile of (arrival minus event time) was about 6 minutes, so 10 minutes leaves room.
steps.code:
val counts = events
    .withWatermark("event_time", "10 minutes")
    .groupBy(window(col("event_time"), "5 minutes"), col("merchant_id"))
    .count()
    .select(col("window.start").alias("window_start"), col("window.end").alias("window_end"),
        col("merchant_id"), col("count").alias("authorizations"))

steps.say: Write final windows once, into Iceberg. Append mode plus Iceberg's batch-id check gives exactly once. A one-minute trigger means one commit a minute instead of one every few seconds.

Watch it. Each micro-batch reports its watermark, the rows in state and the rows dropped as late. Export them to your metrics: state that keeps growing means the watermark isn't cleaning up, and a rising drop count means the delay is too short.
steps.code:
val p = query.lastProgress()
log.info("watermark={} stateRows={} droppedLate={}",
    p.eventTime()["watermark"],
    p.stateOperators()[0].numRowsTotal(),
    p.stateOperators()[0].numRowsDroppedByWatermark())

lab.title: Model the watermark, then run it against Spark
steps: Run the tests. All eleven fail on `TODO`s. `WindowedCounterTest` checks your model on its own; `AuthorizationCountsTest` drives a real Spark stream with a `MemoryStream` (the tests choose exactly which events form each micro-batch, no Kafka needed) and writes to an Iceberg table in a temp folder.

Write `WindowedCounter`: `windowOf` floors a time to its 5-minute window; `batch` drops events whose window ends at or before the current watermark, counts the rest, moves the watermark to the latest event time minus the delay (never back), and emits and forgets the windows that end at or before it.
Write `AuthorizationCounts.perWindow`: watermark, window, count, then flatten the window into `window_start` and `window_end`. Write `start`: append mode, the checkpoint folder, and the Iceberg sink.

The last test feeds the same seven batches to your model and to Spark, and checks that they agree on every watermark, every emitted window and the number of dropped events. If they disagree, the failing batch tells you which rule is off.
Read the replay test: it deletes the newest `commits/` file and restarts the query, and expects no duplicate rows. Which part of the system makes that pass?
hints: Window start: `Instant.ofEpochMilli(ms - Math.floorMod(ms, size.toMillis()))`. A `TreeMap<Instant, Long>` keyed by window start makes the state, and `headMap(watermark.minus(size), true)` gives the windows that are closed.
Keep the latest event time across batches in a field. Check each event against the watermark from before the batch, then update the watermark.
lab.done_when: All eleven tests in `WindowedCounterTest` and `AuthorizationCountsTest` pass.

drill.title: A watermarked count from memory
drill.prompt: From memory, write the Structured Streaming query that counts authorizations per merchant in 5-minute event-time windows, accepts events up to 15 minutes late, and appends final windows to the Iceberg table `lake.fraud.velocity`. Then answer: with the latest event at 11:40, is an event from 11:24 counted? One from 11:26?

answer.src:
events
    .withWatermark("event_time", "15 minutes")        // same column as the window, before groupBy
    .groupBy(window(col("event_time"), "5 minutes"), col("merchant_id"))
    .count()
    .writeStream()
    .format("iceberg")
    .outputMode("append")                            // each window once, when final
    .option("checkpointLocation", "/checkpoints/velocity")
    .toTable("lake.fraud.velocity")

// latest event 11:40, so the watermark is 11:25 (from the next batch on).
// 11:24 is in [11:20, 11:25), which ends at 11:25 <= watermark: closed, dropped.
// 11:26 is in [11:25, 11:30), which ends after 11:25: still open, counted.

recap: Event time is when the event happened; processing time is when you read it. Count by event time, or an outage and its catch-up become fake spikes.
Structured Streaming runs your DataFrame plan on each micro-batch of new input and keeps running aggregates in a state store, checkpointed under the query's folder.
The watermark is the latest event time seen minus the delay you allow. A window is final when the watermark reaches its end: it is written and its state deleted. Later events for it are dropped.
Spark drops a late event by its window's end, not by its own age, and a new watermark applies from the next batch. Data less late than the delay is never dropped.
Append writes each row once when final, update writes changed rows, complete rewrites everything and never drops state. The sink must support the mode.
Exactly once needs a replayable source, a checkpoint and an idempotent or transactional sink. Iceberg skips a replayed batch by its id; a plain `foreachBatch` insert doesn't.

quiz.q: A stream counts authorizations in 5-minute event-time windows with a 10-minute watermark. The latest event so far is 14:32. An event stamped 14:21 arrives. What happens?
options: Counted: its window [14:20, 14:25) ends after the watermark, 14:22
Dropped: it is 11 minutes late, more than the 10 minutes allowed
Counted in the current window, [14:30, 14:35)
The query fails, because the event is older than the watermark
quiz.why: The watermark is 14:32 minus 10 minutes, 14:22. Spark drops a late event only when its window has already closed, and [14:20, 14:25) ends at 14:25, after 14:22, so the window is open and the event is counted. Being older than the delay isn't the test. An event is never moved to another window, and late data never fails the query.

quiz.q: A team's streaming count runs in update mode with no `withWatermark`. Tests pass. What happens in production over the following weeks?
options: Nothing: update mode writes each change, so it doesn't need state
Late events get dropped after the default 10-minute watermark
Every window of every merchant stays in the state store forever, so state and checkpoint time grow until executors run short of memory
Spark refuses to start the query
quiz.why: Without a watermark Spark can never decide a window is final, so it keeps every count in case a late event arrives. Update mode still needs state to know the new count. There is no default watermark. Spark refuses append mode for an aggregation without a watermark, but update and complete start fine, which is why this slips through tests.

quiz.q: Which sink gives exactly-once results when Spark replays a batch after a crash?
options: `foreachBatch` that runs `INSERT INTO ledger_counts SELECT * FROM batch`
The Kafka sink
The Iceberg sink, or a `foreachBatch` that MERGEs on (window, merchant)
Any sink, because the checkpoint guarantees exactly once by itself
quiz.why: After a crash Spark reruns the last uncommitted batch with the same offsets and state. Iceberg records the query and batch id in each snapshot and skips a batch it already committed; a MERGE keyed on the window just overwrites the same values. A plain INSERT appends the batch twice, and Spark's Kafka sink is at-least-once. The checkpoint makes the replay deterministic, but the sink decides whether the replay duplicates.

quiz.q: A dashboard must show the current count of the open 5-minute window and change as events arrive. The sink is a key-value store keyed by (merchant, window). Which output mode?
options: Append, because it is exactly once
Update, because it writes each changed window right away and the sink can overwrite by key
Complete, because the dashboard needs every window
Any: output modes only change performance
quiz.why: Append writes a window only after the watermark closes it, which is minutes too late for a live count. Update writes each window whenever its count changes, and a keyed store turns each write into an overwrite. Complete would rewrite every window ever seen on every batch and never clean state.

quiz.q: From lesson 5: Structured Streaming runs each micro-batch as Spark jobs. The windowed count groups by (window, merchant). Where does a stage boundary fall in each micro-batch, and why?
options: Nowhere: streaming runs one task per event
Before the aggregation: an `Exchange` hash-partitions rows by the grouping key, so each task owns the state of its keys
After the sink write, so the commit log is a stage
Between every two micro-batches only
quiz.why: Grouping is a wide transformation, so the plan has an `Exchange` that hash-partitions rows by (window, merchant) and ends a stage, just as in a batch `groupBy`. The state store is split the same way: the task that receives a key's rows owns that key's running count. That's why the number of state partitions follows `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` and can't change after the first run without resetting the checkpoint.

flashcards.back: The time the event happened, carried in the event (for a payment, when the card was authorized), as opposed to when a consumer read it.

flashcards.front: How does Spark compute the watermark?
flashcards.back: The latest event time seen so far minus the delay given to `withWatermark`. It only moves forward, and a new value applies from the next micro-batch.
When the watermark reaches its end. Then append mode writes it once and Spark deletes its state.

flashcards.front: Which late events does Spark drop?
flashcards.back: Events whose window has already closed (window end at or before the watermark). An event older than the delay is still counted if its window is open.

flashcards.front: What does each output mode write?
flashcards.back: Append: rows once, when final. Update: rows changed in this batch. Complete: the whole result table every batch, with no state cleanup.

flashcards.front: What three things make a stream exactly once end to end?
flashcards.back: A replayable source (Kafka offsets), a checkpoint (offsets, commits, state), and an idempotent or transactional sink.

flashcards.front: Why doesn't a replayed batch duplicate rows in an Iceberg sink?
flashcards.back: Each snapshot records the query id and batch (epoch) id, and the sink skips a batch it has already committed.

terms.plain: When the event happened, as stamped in the event itself.
When the streaming job reads or processes the event.
Fixed, non-overlapping time buckets, such as every 5 minutes from 10:00.
One run of the streaming query over the input that arrived since the last run.
Per-key running values (such as counts per window) kept between micro-batches and saved in the checkpoint.
Latest event time seen minus an allowed delay; windows that end before it are final.
Which result rows each micro-batch writes: append, update or complete.
The folder where a query records offsets, completed batches and state, so a restart resumes exactly.

explain_back.prompt: A colleague asks why the fraud team's per-merchant count spiked at 10:20 and why your event-time version didn't. Explain event time, the watermark and the late event at 10:03 that was still counted, using the stepper's batches.
explain_back.answer: Their version counted events by when the consumer read them. The consumer was down from 10:10 to 10:20 and read the backlog in a minute, so 10 minutes of authorizations landed in the 10:20 bucket and the rule saw 45 in 5 minutes. Ours counts each event in the window of its own timestamp, the time the card was used, so the backlog went back to the 10:10 and 10:15 windows where it belongs. Event time raises a new question: when is a window finished, if a late event can always arrive? The watermark answers it. After each micro-batch Spark takes the latest event time seen, subtracts our allowed delay of 10 minutes, and treats every window that ends at or before that as final: it writes the count once and deletes the window's state, which keeps memory bounded. When 10:14 arrived the watermark became 10:04. Then 10:03 arrived, 11 minutes behind 10:14. It was still counted, because Spark drops a late event only when its window has closed, and [10:00, 10:05) ends at 10:05, after the watermark. When 10:21 arrived, the watermark moved to 10:11 and the first two windows were written. Events for them that arrived afterwards, like 10:04 and 10:08, were dropped and counted in the drop metric, which tells us whether 10 minutes was a good bet.

deeper.body:
Joins between two streams need watermarks on both sides. To join authorizations with captures on `payment_id`, Spark keeps each side's rows in state until a match arrives. Add a watermark to each side and a time condition to the join (`capture_time BETWEEN auth_time AND auth_time + INTERVAL 7 DAYS`), and Spark can drop rows that can no longer match. Without them, the join's state grows forever, like the count without a watermark.

For keyed logic that SQL can't express, such as "flag a card after three declines followed by an approval within 2 minutes", Spark 4.0 added `transformWithState`: you write a processor per key with typed state (values, lists, maps), timers, and a time-to-live for each piece of state. It's the closest Spark gets to Flink's keyed process functions.

State size matters for both engines. Spark's default state store keeps state in executor memory and writes changes to the checkpoint; the RocksDB state store keeps it on local disk and handles much more. Flink 2.0's disaggregated state goes further and keeps the primary copy on object storage, so a job with terabytes of state can rescale without moving it all.

Spark's Real-time Mode trigger, `Trigger.RealTime("5 minutes")`, looks like a latency setting but isn't: the documentation describes the duration mainly as a checkpoint interval. The tasks run continuously and process records as they arrive; the duration says how often progress is checkpointed. Its Kafka sink is at-least-once.
